appraisal_events.evidence: « il me parut diminuer, s’imprégner d’humanité, trouver assez grande pour lui une petite place dans ma mémoire » ; ses revenus féodaux servent « pour avoir cinq automobiles Charron, un hôtel à Paris et un à Londres, une loge le lundi à l’Opéra » ; « il ne différait pas des hommes de même fortune et de même âge qui avaient une moins poétique origine » et « n’avait plus qu’une ambition dans la vie, celle d’être élu membre correspondant de l’Académie des Sciences morales et politiques ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator stages an explicit deflation: the prince's mystical Germanic name, first heard as stained glass and Homeric epithet, shrinks into a familiar spa-town memory and then into an ordinary rich man whose only ambition is an Academy seat, for which he solicits an introduction at Mme de Villeparisis's. The verb « diminuer » is the narrator's own, so the diminishment is endorsed rather than merely reported.

appraisal_events.evidence: Malgré les amabilités, les décorations russes et les citations, « il avait eu devant lui un ingrat […] qui n’avait pas fait avancer sa candidature d’un pas, ne lui avait même pas promis sa voix ! » ; à « Je voudrais bien être votre collègue » Norpois répond seulement « Ah ! je serais très heureux ! » ; le prince conclut : « J’ai compris que j’avais fait fausse route. »
appraisal_events.explanation: Norpois pockets every favor, answers with exquisite politeness and a warm but empty formula, and concedes nothing — a courteous withholding that leaves the soliciting prince, by his own imagined dispatch, defeated. The passage's power arithmetic (Norpois alone commands ten-odd votes, the prince cannot reach six) makes the prince the dependent party.

status_effects.explanation: The poetic aura of his name and titles is explicitly dissolved into banal modern wealth and a petty academic ambition; the narrator names the movement « diminuer ».

His whole campaign of gifts, decorations and diplomatic hinting extracts nothing from Norpois, and he must admit he took the wrong road — though the passage still credits him as « un fin diplomate » rather than a dupe.

Norpois holds the entire exchange on his own terms: he receives the favors, deploys impeccable courtesy and an ambiguous « Ah ! je serais très heureux ! », and commits to nothing, forcing the prince to acknowledge failure.
He is shown as the man who alone disposes of at least a dozen Academy votes and whom a sovereign prince travels to court, which locally raises his standing relative to his suitor.

ambiguities: Mme de Marsantes's « C’est l’antisémitisme en personne » is offered as praise within the salon's code, and the narrator neither comments nor reacts; the text underdetermines whether this locally elevates the prince in that milieu or is left to condemn the speaker, so it is recorded as no separate appraisal event.

« il avait eu devant lui un ingrat » is free indirect discourse voicing the prince's grievance, not the narrator's verdict; read as the narrator's judgment it would blame Norpois, but the surrounding framing of Norpois's imperviousness and of the prince's transactional expectations supports reading it as the prince's ironized complaint, which is why E2 is scored as a gain for Norpois rather than blame.
